Brazil’s National Data Protection Authority (ANPD) has ordered Discord to suspend its "Go Live" feature and all equivalent video streaming tools across the country within three business days.

The platform itself is not blocked. Text chat, voice channels and other core functions remain fully available to Brazilian users. The suspension will stay in place until Discord proves it has implemented effective safeguards to protect children and adolescents.

First Lady Janja da Silva had publicly called for a full ban of the platform days earlier. Discord described the order as "premature," stating it is carefully reviewing the measure, continues to cooperate with law enforcement, and confirmed it quickly removed the private server involved. The company noted that some of the activity was coordinated on other platforms.

Failure to comply could result in fines of up to 50 million reais (approximately $9.7 million) per violation. Discord has 10 business days to appeal. A complete ban of the platform would still require a court decision.

Just moments away from winning an Olympic silver medal, Canadian sailor Larry Lemieux made a decision that would cost him the podium, but save two lives.

During the 1988 Seoul Olympics, Lemieux was running second in the Finn-class sailing event when fierce 35-knot winds capsized a nearby boat carrying two Singaporean sailors. 

Without hesitation, he abandoned his race, rescued both men from the rough seas, and stayed with them until a patrol boat arrived.

By the time he returned to the course, his chance at a medal was gone.

To this day, Larry Lemieux remains the only Canadian ever to receive it.

He told the police the truth about a murder. It cost him 31 YEARS of his life.

Dusty Turner was a young Navy SEAL when a woman was murdered in Virginia in 1995. According to the account of his case, Turner reported that his SEAL swim buddy, Billy Joe Brown, had committed the murder.

Brown turned around and implicated Turner.

Both men were prosecuted. Turner was convicted and sentenced to 82 years in prison.

Then came the part that makes this story almost impossible to stomach.

Years later, Brown admitted that he had lied and that Turner was innocent. In 2008, Brown testified under oath. A judge subsequently found that Turner had no role in the murder or restraint of the victim, and in 2009 Turner was granted a Writ of Actual Innocence.

He should have walked out of prison.

He didn’t.

Virginia appealed, and Turner remained behind bars as the legal battle continued.

Year after year passed.

A man who had once worn the uniform of a Navy SEAL watched his 20s disappear. Then his 30s. Then his 40s. Then his 50s.

Finally, Virginia granted Turner parole in January 2026. He walked out of prison on March 5, 2026, after roughly 31 years behind bars.

There is no check big enough and no apology powerful enough to hand someone three decades of his life back.

Thirty-one years. Think about everything that fits inside 31 years.

That is what makes wrongful convictions so terrifying. When the system gets it wrong, the sentence isn’t served by some statistic on a piece of paper.

A human being serves every single day of it.
